analysis.one_liner: Raises the maximum Pell Grant, extends aid to 15 semesters, and expands food aid for students.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in April 2018 with no cosponsors, died in committee without a markup, vote, or floor action before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The AID Act would raise the maximum Pell Grant to $9,970 and index it to inflation, stretch the lifetime limit from 12 to 15 semesters, and open a new half-size Pell stream for short-term job training programs that lead to credentials employers recognize. It would require colleges to give every federal borrower a detailed annual counseling session and a standardized, consumer-tested 'shopping sheet' comparing costs, debt, and graduation outcomes. It would also repeal the rule that suspends federal student aid after a drug conviction, drop the drug-conviction question from the FAFSA, and loosen SNAP food-stamp rules so more low-income students qualify and no longer lose benefits just because their student loans cover living costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income college students, who would get larger grants and more semesters of eligibility; working adults seeking short-term credentials, who would get a new half-grant; student borrowers, who would get clearer annual counseling and standardized cost-and-outcome disclosures; students with past drug convictions, who would regain access to federal aid; and food-insecure students, who would qualify more easily for SNAP.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the maximum Pell Grant to $9,970 for award year 2019-20 and indexes it to inflation afterward, up from the roughly $6,100 maximum in effect at introduction [S3]
Increases lifetime Pell eligibility from 12 to 15 semesters of full-time study [S3]

Creates a 'job training Pell Grant' worth half the maximum Pell for short-term programs (150-600 clock hours) that lead to credentials recognized by employers, with accreditation safeguards requiring proof the training aligns with local employer needs [S3]

Replaces one-time loan counseling with mandatory annual counseling covering repayment amounts, private-vs-federal loan tradeoffs, and default consequences, plus a standardized, consumer-tested financial aid 'shopping sheet' every college must use as its award letter or cover sheet [S3]
Repeals the Higher Education Act provision suspending Pell Grants, loans, and work study after a drug conviction, and removes the drug-conviction question from the FAFSA [S3]

Expands SNAP for students: lets those with a zero expected family contribution and most independent students qualify, and stops counting living expenses funded by student loans against food-stamp eligibility [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through higher spending on Pell Grants and SNAP, and colleges, which would bear the cost of annual counseling and standardized disclosure requirements. Short-term grant money spent on weak programs would be a wasted cost to taxpayers and to students who use up limited lifetime eligibility.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and college aid offices

drawbacks.text: Short-term Pell expansion has historically risked funding low-quality programs; the bill tries to guard against this by requiring employer-aligned curricula, recognized credentials, and accreditation oversight, but grants still count against a student's limited lifetime eligibility [S3]

Raising the maximum grant without measures to hold down tuition could let colleges absorb part of the increase, and larger federal aid volumes carry real fiscal cost even though the bill includes no cost estimate [S3]
The annual counseling and standardized shopping-sheet requirements impose new administrative work on every college financial aid office, and small institutions would feel that burden most [S3]
Extending eligibility to 15 semesters makes it easier for students to drift through programs slowly, a cost-conscious reformer's objection the bill's longer runway invites [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The student-facing benefits are concrete and well-targeted: bigger and longer grants, clearer loan counseling, restoration of aid to people with old drug convictions, and food aid for hungry students. The main risks are fiscal cost and the quality of the new short-term grant stream, which the bill partially addresses with accreditation and employer-alignment safeguards. On balance the design is sound for students, though the cost to taxpayers is unquantified in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Education and the Workforce and Agriculture Committees and then to a subcommittee, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended, so no vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the AID Act on April 18, 2018 [S1]
No member of the House cosponsored the bill [S4]
The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and the Agriculture Committee on the day of introduction [S5]
On May 22, 2018 it was referred to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Nutrition, and the record shows no further action of any kind through the end of the Congress [S5]
The bill never received a committee markup, a roll-call vote, or floor action in either chamber [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died with no action, colleges avoided new counseling and disclosure mandates, no new federal Pell or SNAP spending was authorized, and private student lenders kept a status quo in which federal borrowers get less complete loan counseling. Low-income students, whose grants would have grown, came out behind.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; colleges avoided new mandates

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the AID Act on April 18, 2018 and proposed raising the maximum Pell Grant, extending eligibility to 15 semesters, mandating annual loan counseling and a standardized shopping sheet, repealing the drug-conviction aid ban, and expanding SNAP for students

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action — no markup, no report, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no committee action, so no partisan pattern appears in the record.

industries.note: Colleges would face new annual counseling and standardized disclosure duties, a real compliance cost, but would also receive a higher maximum Pell and a new short-term grant stream that brings in federal revenue. On net, larger aid flows benefit them while the disclosure rules cut against their preferred flexibility.

The job training Pell Grant creates a new federal funding stream for 8-15 week programs, a category for-profit providers dominate. The bill builds in safeguards — employer-aligned training, recognized credentials, and added accreditation scrutiny — so the risk to students depends on how well those standards are enforced.

Mandatory annual counseling would tell every borrower to exhaust federal loans before considering private ones and explain the differences in bankruptcy treatment, which would steer borrowing toward federal loans and away from private lenders. What is a loss for lenders is a gain for borrowers.
